captions: Let's return to that shared middle block from
the chain rule and give it the spotlight
it deserves.
Here is the question it answers.
If I tell you the value of X,
how much does that shrink your uncertainty about
Y?
Picture two circles.
The left circle is the entropy of X
— the total uncertainty you have about it.
The right circle is the entropy of Y.
Now,
if X and Y are related in any
way,
the two circles overlap.
And that overlap is the whole point of
this beat.
It is called the mutual information between X
and Y — the uncertainty the two variables
share.
Put as plainly as possible:
it is the number of bits you learn
about X,
for free,
just by observing Y.
Written as an equation,
the mutual information equals the entropy of X,
minus the entropy of X once you already
know Y.
It is your uncertainty before,
minus your uncertainty after.
Whatever the observation removed,
that is the information it gave you.
The left crescent — the part of X
that the overlap does not cover — is
what stays uncertain even after you have seen
Y.
And what about two variables that have nothing
to do with each other?
Watch.
The circles drift apart,
the overlap vanishes,
and the mutual information drops to zero.

Independence means knowing one tells you exactly
nothing
about the other.
This single number is quietly everywhere in modern
science.
It measures how much a feature reveals about
a label in machine learning.
How strongly two genes are linked.
How well two signals correlate — capturing curved

relationships that ordinary correlation completely
misses.
And,
as we are about to see,
it measures exactly how much of your message
survives a noisy channel.
